claims.claim: Sadao Hasegawa's work, the review adds, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.
claims.reason: The source says 'Most of the Japanese illustrator's work, you guessed it, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime.' The article drops the quantifier 'Most of' and attributes the unqualified, absolute version to the review ('the review adds'). The source establishes a partial claim; the article states a total one and sources it to the reviewer. This also feeds the closing paragraph, which treats Hasegawa as a case of work that 'went unshown while its maker was alive' without qualification.

claims.claim: Two of those names, taken here not because the review places them above the rest but simply because they can be set beside each other.
claims.reason: This asserts a negative fact about the review's own ranking — that it does not place George and Walter above the other artists. The source does not establish that, and arguably runs the other way: George's story is 'worth telling' and her work 'deserves to be seen far outside the city's confines', and Walter's 'weird little paintings' are said to eclipse the Rose Wylie and Lynette Yiadom-Boakye works around them. The article states as settled a claim about the reviewer's relative valuation that the source does not support.

claims.claim: It is stated as an obligation running two ways at once, and the second direction is the harder one.
claims.reason: The source states the duty ('a duty - to viewers and to their subjects - to tell them clearly') but says nothing about one direction being harder than the other. The comparative judgement is the article's own argument, presented here in flat declarative form as though it were something the review establishes.

claims.claim: There is no map that resolves it.
claims.reason: The source says only that it is 'impossible to figure out how any of it fits together'. That is a claim about legibility, not about the existence or absence of a festival map, programme or guide. Read as metaphor it is close to the source; read literally it asserts a fact about the festival's materials that nothing in the source or packet establishes. Resolving it would require knowing whether EAF publishes a programme/map, which is outside what was given.

claims.claim: without the visitor having brought anything to the encounter except the willingness to walk in
claims.reason: An assertion about the mental state and preparation of gallery visitors generally. The source supports only that a visitor may not have heard of the artists ('some subcultural genius or longlost creative you've never heard of'). Not having heard of an artist is not the same as having brought nothing to the encounter. This is the article's interpretation of the visitor's position, stated as description rather than as argument.

claims.claim: What it does not describe, and cannot, is the other span of time these dates measure: the years in which that same work went unshown while its maker was alive.
claims.reason: For George and Walter the source does establish that the work went unshown in their lifetimes. For Hasegawa it establishes only that MOST of the work did, so the generalisation across all three is broader than the source. The 'and cannot' is also a certainty claim about what the word discovery is capable of describing — the article's own argument, stated as settled rather than as its reading.

Pre-scan false positive. This is the article's title, not a named entity. It is built directly from the source's own phrase 'You've just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like.' The trailing 'By' the pre-scan picked up is a byline artifact, not a claim.

Pre-scan false positive on the possessive form. The source names 'Sadao Hasegawa (1945-1999)' explicitly, so the entity is grounded. The problem with this sentence is the dropped quantifier, flagged separately above, not the name.
